In [[epidemiology]] and [[biostatistics]], the '''experimental event rate (EER)''' is a measure of [[frequency (statistics)|how often]] a particular statistical event (such as response to a drug, [[adverse event]] or death) occurs within the experimental group (non-control group) of an experiment.<ref>{{cite web |url=http://www.medicine.ox.ac.uk/bandolier/booth/glossary/EER.html |title=Experimental event rate (EER) |website=www.medicine.ox.ac.uk |access-date=22 May 2022 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20100820042408/http://www.medicine.ox.ac.uk/bandolier/booth/glossary/EER.html |archive-date=20 August 2010 |url-status=dead}}</ref>

This value is very useful in determining the therapeutic benefit or risk to patients in experimental groups, in comparison to patients in [[placebo]] or traditionally treated control groups.{{cn|date=August 2023}}

Three statistical terms rely on EER for their calculation: [[absolute risk reduction]], [[relative risk reduction]] and [[number needed to treat]].

==Control event rate==
The  ''control event rate (CER)'' is identical to the experimental event rate except that is measured within the [[Scientific control|scientific control group]] of an experiment.<ref>{{cite web |url=http://www.medicine.ox.ac.uk/bandolier/booth/glossary/CER.html |title=Control event rate (CER) |website=www.medicine.ox.ac.uk |access-date=22 May 2022 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20100820043918/http://www.medicine.ox.ac.uk/bandolier/booth/glossary/CER.html |archive-date=20 August 2010 |url-status=dead}}</ref>
